problems.description: Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE in test_app.py and transport.py (2 of the 3 measured violations).
Classes should use PascalCase in test_app.py (measured violation).
_broadcast assigns asyncio.gather results then immediately discards them via `del results`; intentional failure isolation but an awkward idiom a reviewer will flag.
Direct messages accept both `client_id` and `recipient_id` field names, implying a dual/ambiguous message schema that should be pinned down.

Cognitive complexity +9 and a single NotificationServer class mix client registry, message routing, and broadcast concerns, flattening the seed's model/routes/error-handling seams (though the +3-file split partially offsets this).

strengths: Typed async architecture with `from __future__ import annotations` and complete type hints on all public methods.
Concurrency-safe client registry with per-connection cleanup via try/finally and failure-isolated broadcast (return_exceptions=True) so one stale client cannot block others.
Strict message validation with structured system-error responses for malformed JSON, unsupported types, and missing targets.
Removed stale seed stubs (_legacy_format_date, _notify_admin, fetch_task alias) and the seed's status-insertion bug; SonarQube shows smells -2, bugs +0, duplications +0.0%.
Modular split into 3 files including transport.py, a good seam for transport-layer changes.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, fully-typed greenfield rewrite of the Flask seed into an async WebSocket notification service that matches the story intent, held back only by three minor convention violations (0.83) and small maintainability nits.

problems.description: The set literal {"subscribe", "unsubscribe"} is duplicated twice in _handle_message; define a module-level SUBSCRIPTION_TYPES constant beside MESSAGE_TYPES to match the file's own constant pattern.
_channel_from accepts the channel in two places (top-level 'channel' or payload.channel), making the wire protocol ambiguous; the tests even exercise both forms. Pick one canonical location.
tests/test_app.py adds 'import asyncio' after 'import json' (stdlib imports should be alphabetized), and the pre-existing __import__('asyncio').sleep(0) hack could now use the imported module.
Trailing whitespace before '}' in list_subscribers: 'sorted(self.channels.get(name, ())) }'.
The 'health' aiohttp app now also serves the channel management API (/channels, /channels/{name}/subscribers); the name no longer describes the surface as it grows.

strengths: Extends the existing class cleanly, reusing _broadcast, _message, _send_system and the MESSAGE_TYPES constant pattern rather than inventing new machinery
Correct lifecycle handling: disconnect removes the client from every channel subscriber set and prunes empty channels
Strong test coverage including the negative case (non-subscriber must NOT receive) and empty-channel cleanup assertions
Typed signatures, deterministic sorted output, and preservation of the existing 'del results' gather pattern
commit_reviews.summary: A well-integrated, well-tested channel-subscription feature that respects the NotificationServer's existing patterns, held back only by minor nits (duplicated set literal, dual-location channel field, import order) and a convention score understated by analyzer noise from files that postdate this commit.

problems.description: Synchronous sqlite3 execute()/commit() in _persist() runs on the asyncio event loop on every message, blocking all client handling; use aiosqlite or an executor. (Cognitive complexity +48 in the same commit corroborates the code is doing too much per handler.)

Resource lifecycle is inconsistent: the SQLite connection is opened eagerly in __init__ (_open_database) and never closed (no shutdown/teardown path visible), while the Redis connection/task is deferred to _connect_redis and its cancellation/reconnect story is untracked.

Cross-instance delivery routes every message through a full pub/sub round-trip — the publishing instance relies on its own _redis_listener to self-deliver, making local delivery dependent on listener health and adding duplicate-delivery/ordering surface (dedup only via INSERT OR IGNORE).

No tests added (+0 files) for substantial new behavior: Redis pub/sub fallback, SQLite persistence, and channel membership in Redis are all untested; _connect_redis has no visible call site in the diff to confirm it is ever exercised.

Direct-message routing queries the 'notification:clients' set with sismember, but no sadd into that set appears in the diff — remote-target lookups may always fail unless registration populates it (verify in the truncated portion).

_handle_message uses conditional re-assignment of target_exists/subscribed (bool redefined per Redis state), and _open_database parses URLs via magic string slicing ([9:]/[10:]) instead of urllib.parse — brittle and hard to follow.
Hot path performs json.dumps per publish/persist plus a synchronous commit() per message; a 0.5s socket_timeout on Redis makes delivery dependent on Redis latency rather than only availability.

strengths: Graceful degradation: Redis connect failures (short timeouts, RedisError/OSError/TimeoutError) fall back to local _deliver_message via the _redis_enabled flag, keeping the server functional without Redis.
Reuses existing delivery helpers (_deliver_message, _broadcast, _send_system) and extracts _message_dict, respecting the file's established structure rather than adding parallel paths.
Idempotent persistence via INSERT OR IGNORE keyed on a stable message id — a sound dedup strategy for the pub/sub duplicate-delivery risk.
Uses redis.asyncio, consistent with the existing async aiohttp/websockets stack.

Commit introduces no new measured convention violations — the three reported (test_app.py, transport.py) are in files this diff does not touch, so the 0.83 score reflects pre-existing debt, not this change.
commit_reviews.summary: The integration adds real capability (SQLite persistence + Redis fan-out) with a clean fallback path and consistent use of existing helpers, but it accrues debt via blocking sync SQLite on the event loop, an untracked resource lifecycle, and zero test coverage for the new subsystems.

problems.description: The pluggable-transport abstraction is only half realized: `handler` still receives the raw WebSocket connection (typed `Any`) and `on_connect(client_id, websocket)` forwards it, so the server remains coupled to the websocket lifecycle; the `TRANSPORT` env gate raises `ValueError` for anything but "websocket", so no second transport can actually be selected yet.
Concrete type hints (`Server`, `ServerConnection`) were replaced with `Any` on `self.websocket_server` and `handler`, erasing static type safety exactly where the new abstraction seam is introduced.
`self.clients = transport.clients` aliases the transport's own dict, splitting ownership of client state between the server and the transport.
transport.py: module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE (measured).
test_app.py: classes should use PascalCase and module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE (measured).

strengths: Centralizes per-client sends, system messages, and broadcast into a single transport seam (`send_message`/`broadcast`), removing the scattered `client.send(...)` calls.
Drops app.py's direct dependency on the `websockets` library, decoupling core message routing from the transport library.
Zero new SonarQube bugs/smells/duplications, only +4 cognitive complexity; the diff preserves the existing async method structure and docstring style.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive refactor that centralizes message delivery behind a transport abstraction and removes the websockets import from app.py, but the abstraction is only half-complete (websocket-coupled handler, single supported transport) and pays for it with `Any` type erasure and minor naming-convention violations in transport.py and test_app.py.

problems.description: `_local_rate_limits` dict grows unboundedly — entries for clients that stop sending are never evicted, a slow memory leak on a long-running server.
Rate limiting is implemented twice (Redis INCR+EXPIRE path and in-memory window fallback), duplicating the windowing/limit logic and creating divergence risk when one path is tuned.
Hourly `DELETE FROM messages WHERE timestamp < ?` runs a full-table scan on an unindexed column; cost grows with retained history (no index on timestamp).
The /history `since` filter is not covered by tests, and the rate-limit tests exercise only the in-memory fallback path — the Redis counter path is untested.

Static analysis reports 3 convention violations (convention score 0.83): 2 in test_app.py, 1 in transport.py — note transport.py was not modified by this commit, so its flag is pre-existing; the test_app.py flags could not be reproduced in the actual file (no module-level classes or constants exist).

strengths: All five Session-5 requirements implemented: per-client rate limiting with error-return (no drop), paginated /history with has_more, and TTL-based message expiry.
Background-task lifecycle handled correctly — cleanup_task created in start(), cancelled via asyncio.gather in stop(), mirroring the existing redis_task pattern.
Graceful degradation preserved: falls back to local rate limiting when Redis is unavailable, and config parsing falls back to defaults on invalid env values.
Respects the story's architecture: error responses reuse _send_system, the new route joins the existing health_app router, and the transport layer + pub/sub are left intact per constraints.
Tests pass (11/11) and no new dependencies, bugs, or smells added (SonarQube delta: bugs +0, smells +0).
commit_reviews.summary: A solid Session-5 feature commit that delivers rate limiting, history pagination, and message expiry cleanly within the existing single-class server patterns, though it adds minor maintenance debt (unbounded in-memory limiter, duplicated rate-limit logic, unindexed cleanup delete) and leaves the Redis rate-limit and since-filter paths untested.

compounding_issues: Session 1 fully discarded the Flask Todo seed in a greenfield rewrite, forfeiting the seed's models/routes scaffold; the domain mismatch was unavoidable, but none of the seed's structure (e.g. storage separation) was carried into the new async design
Repo hygiene debt accumulated and never repaid: __pycache__ .pyc bytecode was committed in sessions 2, 3, and 5, and a binary messages.db was committed in session 5

NotificationServer remained a monolith — transport, SQLite persistence, Redis state, and (later) rate limiting all lived in one ~450-line class; session 4's transport extraction was the right mitigation but left storage and rate-limit logic inline

The TRANSPORT env knob hard-fails with ValueError on any unsupported value rather than degrading, and the base transport's start() is a silent no-op, so the pluggable abstraction from session 4 was never exercised by a second implementation
key_decisions: Greenfield rewrite of the seed into an async WebSocket notification server (websockets transport + aiohttp health endpoint), committing to asyncio-first design in session 1
Channel subscription model (subscribe/unsubscribe message types + channel-filtered routing) layered onto the message-routing core in session 2
Redis pub/sub fan-out + SQLite persistence in session 3, with soft-fail degradation (short socket connect timeout, in-process delivery fallback when Redis is absent)
Pluggable transport abstraction (BaseTransport ABC + WebSocketTransport) in session 4, decoupling the server from the websockets library
Cross-cutting operational hardening in session 5: Redis-backed per-client rate limiting with local fallback, TTL-based message expiry loop, and a cursor-paginated history endpoint
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across all five sessions. The build was fully green at every checkpoint (4→6→8→8→11 tests passed with zero regressions), each session layering one natural concern — core routing, channel subscriptions, Redis/SQLite integration, transport refactor, and cross-cutting hardening — onto the prior commit. Session 4's transport extraction was the highest-quality move, cleanly separating delivery mechanics from server logic, and session 5 rounded out the service with operational concerns (rate limiting, TTL expiry, history) that a production notification system needs. The main blemishes are cosmetic-to-moderate: committed bytecode and database artifacts, an incompletely decomposed monolith, and a transport abstraction that only ever had one implementation.
story_review.summary: A textbook incremental multi-session build — coherent feature layering with monotonic, regression-free test growth (4→11) from greenfield core through integration, a clean transport refactor, and cross-cutting hardening, marred only by repository hygiene debt and an incompletely decomposed monolith.
